A molecular-dynamics run produces a file with thousands of structures in it, and a student's first instinct is to average something over them and compare it with the average of another run. That instinct produces most of the statistical errors in the simulation literature, because consecutive frames of a trajectory are not independent observations: a nanosecond of sampling can contain fewer than ten independent configurations. This unit takes six real simulations of the Trp-cage miniprotein - two temperatures, three replicas each - and treats their output exactly as what it is, a short, strongly autocorrelated multivariate time series. We measure how much information it actually contains, decide what to discard, compare the conditions in the two possible ways and watch them disagree by twenty-four orders of magnitude in the p-value, and then do the same careful accounting for fluctuations, projections, free-energy surfaces and cluster representatives.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad analiza la salida de una simulación de dinámica molecular como lo que es: una serie temporal corta y fuertemente autocorrelacionada. Con seis trayectorias reales de la miniproteína Trp-cage (dos temperaturas, tres réplicas cada una, 1 ns) se calculan la función de autocorrelación, el tiempo de autocorrelación integrado, la ineficiencia estadística y el tamaño de muestra efectivo; se promedia por bloques y se construye el gráfico de Flyvbjerg-Petersen; se detecta la equilibración con el promedio acumulado inverso y con el criterio de Chodera. El experimento central compara las dos condiciones de dos maneras: con las 3.000 tramas individuales (p del orden de 1e-26) y con las tres réplicas independientes (p = 0,69); la segunda es la honesta, porque la dispersión entre réplicas a la misma temperatura supera la diferencia entre temperaturas. Después se tratan las fluctuaciones por residuo como un problema de comparaciones múltiples, se reducen las coordenadas con PCA y con un tICA implementado a mano, se lee un histograma bidimensional como superficie de energía libre con incertidumbre por bootstrap de bloques, y se agrupan las tramas para extraer estructuras representativas. La conclusión es siempre la misma: el número de réplicas, y no el número de tramas, determina lo que se puede afirmar.

Learning objectives

  • Treat molecular-dynamics observables (RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, distances, hydrogen bonds, energies) as correlated time series: autocorrelation function, integrated autocorrelation time, statistical inefficiency, effective sample size and block averaging.
  • Assess equilibration and convergence (reverse cumulative averaging, Chodera's automated detection, replica agreement) and decide what to discard.
  • Compute uncertainties correctly across replicas and report them, applying the tests of Unit 8 to replica-level rather than frame-level data.
  • Reduce and cluster a conformational ensemble (PCA on Cartesian coordinates, tICA, k-means on the projection), read free-energy-like landscapes critically and attach sampling error to them.
  • Report energy decompositions of the MM/GBSA type with the statistics that hundreds of simultaneous per-residue comparisons demand.

How to read this notebook

Read it linearly with the code running; every number quoted in the prose comes from a cell of this notebook. No simulation is run here and no trajectory file is parsed: the six runs arrive as frozen tables (md_trpcage_observables.csv, md_trpcage_rmsf.csv, md_trpcage_ca_coords.npz), so the notebook needs only NumPy[31], pandas, SciPy[32], matplotlib[26], scikit-learn and statsmodels[30]. In Google Colab run !pip install statsmodels if it is missing. The data folder also contains md_trpcage_strideA1.xtc and md_trpcage_protein.pdb, a 100-frame protein-only trajectory for students who want to repeat the measurements with MDTraj[8] or MDAnalysis[7] in their own environment; those packages are not required here. The unit uses the estimation vocabulary of Unit 7, the testing vocabulary of Unit 8 and the clustering of Unit 15.

1. What a production run leaves behind

Domain context

Molecular dynamics (MD) integrates Newton's equations for every atom of a protein and its surrounding water, with forces given by an empirical energy function called a force field (here AMBER ff14SB[12] with TIP3P-FB water). A frame is the set of atomic coordinates saved at one instant - here every 2 picoseconds (ps), so a 1 nanosecond (ns) run leaves 500 frames. A replica is an independent repetition of the same simulation started with different random velocities; replicas differ because the dynamics are chaotic. The system here is Trp-cage, a designed 20-residue miniprotein[13] used as a test system since 2002 because it folds on the microsecond scale[14] - fast for a protein, still a thousand times longer than the runs analysed here. The quantities extracted per frame are: RMSD, the root-mean-square deviation of the C-alpha atoms from a reference structure after optimal superposition (a scalar measure of "how far the fold has moved", in nm); Rg, the radius of gyration (compactness); the number of backbone hydrogen bonds; helix fraction, the proportion of residues assigned to a helix by the DSSP algorithm[15]; a side-chain distance defining the hydrophobic "cage"; and the thermostat and barostat readouts (instantaneous temperature, box volume, potential energy). RMSF is the root-mean-square fluctuation of one residue around its own average position - a per-residue measure of flexibility, not of displacement.

The six runs were produced with OpenMM 8[10][11] for this course: 4,810 atoms in a cubic box, 50 ps of NVT and 100 ps of NPT equilibration, then 1 ns of production sampling in the NPT ensemble, at 300 K (condition A) and 340 K (condition B), three seeds each. The protocol follows the current best-practice recommendations for foundations in molecular simulation[29]. The question they are meant to answer is the one a thesis student asks every week: does the protein behave differently at the higher temperature? Everything below is about answering that honestly with 1 ns of sampling - and about discovering how little 1 ns is.

Figure 1. The raw material: C-alpha RMSD against time for the six runs. Within a condition the three replicas occupy clearly different bands - at 300 K the means are 0.110, 0.160 and 0.251 nm - and each trace wanders slowly, with excursions lasting tens to hundreds of picoseconds. Neither panel shows unfolding (RMSD stays below 0.3 nm); what they show is that each replica settled into its own region of conformational space and stayed there for the whole nanosecond.

Two features of Figure 1 decide the statistics of the whole unit. The traces are slow: a point is very similar to the point 20 ps before it, so the 500 frames of a run are not 500 observations. And the replicas disagree: the spread between replicas of the same condition (0.110 to 0.251 nm at 300 K) is larger than any difference the eye can find between the two conditions. 2. Frames are not samples: autocorrelation and effective sample size

For a stationary time series $x_1,\dots,x_N$ with mean $\bar{x}$, the normalised autocorrelation function at lag $k$ is

$$C(k) = \frac{\frac{1}{N-k}\sum_{t=1}^{N-k}(x_t-\bar{x})(x_{t+k}-\bar{x})}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}(x_t-\bar{x})^2},$$

with $C(0) = 1$. It answers "how much does a frame still tell me about a frame $k$ steps later?". Summing it gives the statistical inefficiency

$$g = 1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{k_{\max}} C(k),$$

the number of frames one must take to obtain one independent observation, and therefore the effective sample size $N_{\text{eff}} = N/g$. The correct standard error of the mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{eff}}}$, not $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$ - an error of a factor $\sqrt{g}$, which in this data is between 3 and 9. The integrated autocorrelation time in physical units is $\tau_{\text{int}} = \Delta t\,(\tfrac{1}{2} + \sum_{k\ge 1}C(k))$, so that $g = 2\tau_{\text{int}}/\Delta t$. The sum is truncated at the first zero crossing of $C(k)$, because beyond it the estimator is pure noise[1][2].

Worked example: the autocorrelation of six numbers by hand

Take the series 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (mean 3.5; deviations -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, +0.5, +1.5, +2.5). The denominator is 6.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 6.25 = 17.5, so the variance term is 17.5/6 = 2.9167. For lag 1 the five products are (-2.5)(-1.5) = 3.75, (-1.5)(-0.5) = 0.75, (-0.5)(0.5) = -0.25, (0.5)(1.5) = 0.75 and (1.5)(2.5) = 3.75, summing to 8.75; dividing by N - k = 5 gives 1.75. Hence C(1) = 1.75/2.9167 = 0.600. A monotone series is strongly autocorrelated, as it must be. The cell below reproduces the three numbers and then applies the same estimator, in its fast Fourier-transform form, to the real trajectories.

def acf(x, nlags=None):
    '''Normalised autocorrelation function via FFT; C(0) = 1.'''
    x = np.asarray(x, float) - np.mean(x)
    n = len(x); nlags = n - 1 if nlags is None else nlags
    f = np.fft.rfft(x, 2 * n)
    c = np.fft.irfft(f * np.conj(f))[:n].real
    c /= np.arange(n, 0, -1)            # unbiased 1/(N-k) normalisation
    return (c / c[0])[:nlags + 1]

toy = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6.])
dev = toy - toy.mean()
print("by hand : var term = %.4f, lag-1 covariance = %.4f, C(1) = %.3f"
      % ((dev ** 2).sum() / 6, (dev[:-1] * dev[1:]).sum() / 5, ((dev[:-1] * dev[1:]).sum() / 5) / ((dev ** 2).sum() / 6)))
print("by code : C(1) = %.3f" % acf(toy, 2)[1])

def tau_g_neff(x, dt=DT):
    '''Integrated autocorrelation time (ps), statistical inefficiency and effective sample size.'''
    c = acf(x, len(x) // 2)
    zero = int(np.argmax(c <= 0)) if np.any(c <= 0) else len(c)
    s = c[1:zero].sum()
    tau = dt * (0.5 + s); g = 1 + 2 * s
    return tau, g, len(x) / g, zero * dt

by hand : var term = 2.9167, lag-1 covariance = 1.7500, C(1) = 0.600
by code : C(1) = 0.600

Two things deserve attention in that table. First the physics: the integrated autocorrelation time of the C-alpha RMSD is 18 to 85 ps depending on the replica, so the 500 frames of a 1 ns run contain between 5.9 and 27.6 independent observations. The naive standard error, 0.0005-0.0015 nm, under-estimates the real one by a factor $\sqrt{g}$ of 4.3 to 9.2. (With $\Delta t$ = 2 ps the columns $\tau$ and $g$ coincide numerically, because $g = 2\tau/\Delta t$.) Any error bar on an MD average that was computed as $\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{frames}}}$ is wrong by about that factor, and it is wrong in the dangerous direction.

Second the bookkeeping: the frozen summary file reports autocorrelation times about twice as large as ours (137.96 ps against 76.95 ps for run A1) and effective sample sizes correspondingly smaller, because it uses the convention $\tau = \Delta t\,(1 + 2\sum_k C(k))$ - our $g$ expressed in time units - with a biased normalisation of the autocorrelation estimator. Both appear in the literature and in simulation software. The lesson is not that one is right - it is that "the autocorrelation time is 70 ps" is an incomplete statement: give the definition, the truncation rule and the frame interval, or give $N_{\text{eff}}$ directly, which is unambiguous.

Exercise 1

Compute the integrated autocorrelation time of n_hbonds, helix_fraction and potential_energy_kJ_mol for run A1 with tau_g_neff. Which observable decorrelates fastest, and why would you expect the potential energy of a 4,810-atom system to be the fastest of all? What does that imply about using the potential energy as evidence that a simulation is "converged"?

3. Block averaging and the Flyvbjerg-Petersen plot

The autocorrelation route needs a truncation rule. A route that needs none is block averaging: cut the series into $M$ consecutive blocks of length $b$, average within each block, and compute the standard error of those $M$ block means. As $b$ grows past the correlation time the block means become independent and the estimated standard error stops growing; the plateau value is the honest error bar. Plotting it against $b$ is the Flyvbjerg-Petersen construction[3], and the shape of the curve is itself a diagnostic: if no plateau is reached before the blocks become too few to estimate anything, the run is too short for the quantity being measured.

def block_se(x, b):
    '''Standard error of the mean from blocks of length b (frames).'''
    x = np.asarray(x, float); m = len(x) // b
    if m < 2:
        return np.nan
    means = x[:m * b].reshape(m, b).mean(axis=1)
    return means.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(m)

bs = np.array([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100])
tab = {}
for run in RUNS:
    x = obs[(obs["condition"] == run[0]) & (obs["replica"] == int(run[1]))]["rmsd_ca_nm"].to_numpy()
    tab[run] = [block_se(x, b) for b in bs]
blk = pd.DataFrame(tab, index=[f"{int(b*DT)} ps" for b in bs]).round(5)
print("standard error of the mean RMSD (nm) as a function of block length:")
print(blk.to_string())
print("\nfor comparison, sigma/sqrt(N_eff) from section 2:")
print(corr["se_correct"].round(5).to_string())

Figure 3. Block-averaged standard error against block length for the six runs; dotted lines mark the autocorrelation-based estimate sigma/sqrt(N_eff) of section 2. The curves rise steadily and none flattens before 200 ps blocks, where only five blocks remain and the estimate itself becomes erratic - run A2 drops from 0.0017 to 0.0007 nm between the last two points, which is noise, not convergence. Where the two estimators can be compared they agree reasonably (0.0134 against 0.0138 nm for run B2, 0.0054 against 0.0061 nm for A1) and both stand a factor of 4 to 9 above the naive sigma/sqrt(500) that most papers report.

A curve that has not plateaued is not a failure of the method; it is the method reporting that one nanosecond does not resolve the slowest motion contributing to this observable. The honest responses are to extend the simulation, to run more replicas, or to report an error bar derived from the replicas rather than from within a single run - which is what section 6 does, and what reviewers of simulation papers now expect[2][5].

4. Equilibration: deciding what to discard

The beginning of a production run is contaminated by relaxation from the starting structure. Two standard tools decide where that contamination ends. The reverse cumulative average plots the mean of the series computed from time $t_0$ to the end, as a function of $t_0$: while the system is still relaxing the curve drifts, and it flattens once the remaining data are stationary. Chodera's automated criterion[4] formalises the trade-off - discarding data removes bias but costs samples - by choosing the $t_0$ that maximises the effective sample size $N_{\text{eff}}(t_0) = (N - t_0)/g(t_0)$ of the retained portion.

def chodera_t0(x, dt=DT, step=5):
    '''Discard point maximising the effective sample size of the retained data (Chodera 2016).'''
    n = len(x); best_t0, best_neff = 0, -np.inf
    for t0 in range(0, int(0.6 * n), step):
        seg = x[t0:]
        if len(seg) < 50:
            break
        neff = len(seg) / tau_g_neff(seg)[1]
        if neff > best_neff:
            best_t0, best_neff = t0, neff
    return best_t0 * dt, best_neff

eq = []
for run in RUNS:
    x = obs[(obs["condition"] == run[0]) & (obs["replica"] == int(run[1]))]["rmsd_ca_nm"].to_numpy()
    t0, neff = chodera_t0(x)
    eq.append(dict(run=run, t0_ps=t0, n_eff_after=neff, mean_all=x.mean(), mean_after=x[int(t0 / DT):].mean(),
                   shift_nm=x[int(t0 / DT):].mean() - x.mean()))
eq = pd.DataFrame(eq).set_index("run")
print(eq.round(4).to_string())
print("\nmean |shift| caused by discarding: %.4f nm; largest %.4f nm (run %s)"
      % (eq["shift_nm"].abs().mean(), eq["shift_nm"].abs().max(), eq["shift_nm"].abs().idxmax()))

Figure 4. Left: reverse cumulative averages. Four of the six runs are flat from the first frame - their 150 ps of equilibration was enough - while A1 drifts upwards and B3 downwards, by about 0.01 nm. The practical conclusion for this data set is that equilibration detection changes the means by at most 0.013 nm, an order of magnitude less than the between-replica spread of 0.14 nm. We therefore keep all 500 production frames of every run, and say so. That decision must be made and reported once, before the comparison between conditions - choosing a discard point per condition after looking at the comparison is a way of manufacturing a difference, and is the simulation version of the analytic flexibility that Unit 8 warns about.

5. The centrepiece: frame-level versus replica-level testing

Now the question the simulations were run to answer. Does the C-alpha RMSD differ between 300 K and 340 K? There are two ways to ask it with the same data.

The frame-level test pools all 1,500 frames of condition A against all 1,500 frames of condition B and runs Welch's t-test[25]. The replica-level test first reduces each run to one number - its mean - and compares three numbers against three. The first treats frames as independent samples, which section 2 proved they are not: the effective number of independent configurations per condition is about 20 to 60, not 1,500, and even that counts correlated replicas separately. The second treats the replica as the experimental unit, which it is: replicas differ by their random seed exactly as biological replicates differ by their subject.

A = obs.loc[obs["condition"] == "A", "rmsd_ca_nm"].to_numpy()
B = obs.loc[obs["condition"] == "B", "rmsd_ca_nm"].to_numpy()
t_frame, p_frame = stats.ttest_ind(A, B, equal_var=False)
print("FRAME-LEVEL  : n = %d vs %d frames, means %.4f vs %.4f nm, Welch t = %.2f, p = %.3e"
      % (len(A), len(B), A.mean(), B.mean(), t_frame, p_frame))

means = obs.groupby(["condition", "replica"], observed=True)["rmsd_ca_nm"].mean().unstack()
a, b = means.loc["A"].to_numpy(), means.loc["B"].to_numpy()
t_rep, p_rep = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
print("REPLICA-LEVEL: n = 3 vs 3 replica means %s vs %s" % (np.round(a, 4), np.round(b, 4)))
print("               means %.4f +/- %.4f vs %.4f +/- %.4f nm (SE over replicas), Welch t = %.3f, p = %.4f"
      % (a.mean(), a.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(3), b.mean(), b.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(3), t_rep, p_rep))
print("\nratio of p-values: %.3g" % (p_rep / p_frame))
print("within-condition spread at 300 K: %.3f nm; difference between condition means: %.3f nm"
      % (a.max() - a.min(), abs(a.mean() - b.mean())))

REPLICA-LEVEL: n = 3 vs 3 replica means [0.1098 0.1595 0.2515] vs [0.1211 0.1884 0.1504]

within-condition spread at 300 K: 0.142 nm; difference between condition means: 0.020 nm

The frame-level test returns p of order $10^{-26}$ and the replica-level test returns p = 0.69 on the same numbers. Only one of them answers the scientific question. The frame-level test is not "more sensitive"; it is answering a different and uninteresting question - "do these 3,000 particular configurations come from the same distribution?" - with an n inflated fifty-fold by correlation. Its p-value would keep shrinking if the frames were saved every 0.2 ps instead of every 2 ps, without a single new configuration being sampled. That is the signature of a pseudo-replication error[5].

The honest answer is the second one: with three replicas per condition, a difference of 0.02 nm cannot be distinguished from the 0.14 nm spread between replicas at the same temperature. Trp-cage melts experimentally near 315 K but on the microsecond time scale[14], so one nanosecond at 340 K should not show unfolding - and does not.

Reading the table row by row is the habit to acquire. Five structural observables have frame-level p-values between $10^{-12}$ and $10^{-30}$ and replica-level p-values between 0.36 and 0.88: every one of them would be reported as a "significant effect of temperature" by the frame-level analysis, and none of them survives the honest test. The two instrument readouts behave in the opposite way - they are significant by both routes, because the thermostat and the barostat impose them identically in every replica. A results table of this shape, with both columns shown, is far more convincing to a reviewer than a single column of stars[2].

Exercise 2

Subsample each run by taking every fifth frame (100 frames per run instead of 500) and repeat both tests. The replica-level p-value should barely move; the frame-level one should rise by orders of magnitude. Explain in one sentence why the "significance" of the frame-level test is a property of the output-writing frequency rather than of the physics, and what that implies about trajectories saved every 0.1 ps.

6. Error bars from replicas

Once the replica is accepted as the unit of analysis, the recipe is short and is the one used in the group's papers. Compute the observable per replica, average the replica values, and build the interval from the spread of those values with $n = $ number of replicas:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \text{CI}_{95\%} = \bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\,\mathrm{SE},$$

with $t_{0.975,2} = 4.303$ for three replicas - more than twice the 1.96 of a large sample, which is what three replicas cost. The frames inside a replica are used only to compute $x_i$; they never enter the error bar.

def replica_ci(values, conf=0.95):
    v = np.asarray(values, float); n = len(v)
    se = v.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
    h = stats.t.ppf(0.5 + conf / 2, n - 1) * se
    return v.mean(), se, v.mean() - h, v.mean() + h

for cond in "AB":
    m, se, lo, hi = replica_ci(means.loc[cond].to_numpy())
    print("condition %s: mean RMSD %.4f nm, SE %.4f, 95%% CI [%.4f, %.4f]  (t_0.975,2 = %.3f)"
          % (cond, m, se, lo, hi, stats.t.ppf(0.975, 2)))
d = means.loc["B"].to_numpy().mean() - means.loc["A"].to_numpy().mean()
pooled = np.sqrt(means.loc["A"].to_numpy().var(ddof=1) / 3 + means.loc["B"].to_numpy().var(ddof=1) / 3)
print("\ndifference B - A = %+.4f nm, SE %.4f, 95%% CI [%+.4f, %+.4f]"
      % (d, pooled, d - 4.303 * pooled, d + 4.303 * pooled))
sd_rep = np.std(np.concatenate([means.loc["A"].to_numpy() - means.loc["A"].to_numpy().mean(),
                                means.loc["B"].to_numpy() - means.loc["B"].to_numpy().mean()]), ddof=1)
for target in [0.02, 0.05, 0.10]:
    n_needed = 2 * (2.8 * sd_rep / target) ** 2      # rough n per group for 80 % power, two-sided alpha = 0.05
    print("to detect a %.2f nm difference with 80 %% power one needs about %.0f replicas per condition"
          % (target, np.ceil(n_needed)))

The 95 % interval for the 300 K mean runs from 0.0 to 0.35 nm: with three replicas and this much spread, the data constrain the mean RMSD hardly at all. The interval for the difference includes zero by a wide margin. The power calculation at the end says what would be needed: detecting a 0.05 nm difference at 80 % power requires on the order of sixteen replicas of this length, and a 0.02 nm difference about a hundred. That number - not the number of frames - is the one to put in a computing-time proposal, and it is why the field has moved from "one long run" to "many independent runs"[5][21].

7. Per-residue fluctuations: twenty tests at once

The RMSF table gives one number per residue per run: 20 residues x 6 runs. Comparing the conditions residue by residue is twenty simultaneous tests, and the multiple-comparison machinery of Unit 8 applies without modification. With three replicas per condition each individual test has almost no power, so the interesting output is not a list of significant residues but the honest statement that the data do not support one.

Figure 6. Left: per-residue C-alpha RMSF with the standard error over the three replicas. The familiar shape is there - the termini and the Gly-Gly-Pro loop fluctuate most - and the 340 K bars are on average 25 % higher (0.0743 against 0.0594 nm). This is a textbook demonstration of two statistical facts at once. A systematic 25 % increase that is visible in every replica is still not significant when each residue is tested with three values per group, because the between-replica variance is large and a t-test on n = 3 needs a very large effect. And testing twenty residues multiplies the chance of a false positive, so the Benjamini-Hochberg correction[24] pushes the adjusted values further up. The right report is therefore: "mean C-alpha RMSF increased from 0.059 to 0.074 nm at 340 K; with three replicas no individual residue reached significance after FDR correction", possibly with a global test on the mean RMSF rather than twenty local ones - fewer tests, more power, and an answer to the question that was actually asked.

8. Projections: principal components and tICA

A frame of this system is 20 C-alpha positions, that is a point in 60-dimensional space; all six runs together are a 3,000 x 60 matrix, already superposed on the same reference. Principal component analysis finds the orthogonal directions of largest positional variance - in the simulation literature this is called essential dynamics[16] - and projecting the frames onto the first two gives the picture everybody draws. The caveat that must accompany that picture was published almost as early as the method itself: with short trajectories the leading components are dominated by the slowest motion that happened to occur, and projections of different runs can look like different states purely from lack of sampling[17][18].

Time-lagged independent component analysis (tICA) changes the objective: instead of maximising variance it maximises autocorrelation at a chosen lag time, so its leading components are the slowest collective coordinates rather than the widest[6]. It is the standard first step of Markov-state modelling[22][23]. The implementation is a generalised eigenvalue problem and fits in fifteen lines, which is what the next cell does - no specialised package is needed to understand it.

X = np.concatenate([npz[r] for r in RUNS]).reshape(6 * 500, -1)     # (3000, 60), already superposed
run_of = np.repeat(RUNS, 500)
time_of = np.tile(npz["time_ps"], 6)
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
pca = PCA(n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(Xc)
Y = pca.transform(Xc)
print("PCA explained variance ratio:", np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:5], 3),
      "| first three together: %.3f" % pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:3].sum())
print("\nmean position of each run on PC1 / PC2 (nm):")
for r in RUNS:
    m = run_of == r
    print("   %s  PC1 %+.3f (sd %.3f)   PC2 %+.3f" % (r, Y[m, 0].mean(), Y[m, 0].std(), Y[m, 1].mean()))

mean position of each run on PC1 / PC2 (nm):
   A1  PC1 -0.330 (sd 0.097)   PC2 -0.045
   A2  PC1 -0.037 (sd 0.093)   PC2 +0.269
   A3  PC1 +0.595 (sd 0.096)   PC2 -0.055
   B1  PC1 -0.262 (sd 0.111)   PC2 -0.050
   B2  PC1 +0.197 (sd 0.221)   PC2 +0.177
   B3  PC1 -0.162 (sd 0.130)   PC2 -0.296

def tica(Z, groups, lag):
    '''Hand-rolled tICA: whiten with the instantaneous covariance, diagonalise the symmetrised time-lagged one.'''
    C0 = np.zeros((Z.shape[1],) * 2); Ct = np.zeros_like(C0); n = 0
    for g in np.unique(groups):
        W = Z[groups == g]; W = W - W.mean(axis=0)
        a, b = W[:-lag], W[lag:]
        C0 += a.T @ a + b.T @ b
        Ct += a.T @ b + b.T @ a
        n += 2 * len(a)
    C0 /= n; Ct /= n
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(C0); w = np.maximum(w, 1e-12)
    Wh = V @ np.diag(w ** -0.5) @ V.T                 # whitening matrix
    M = Wh @ Ct @ Wh
    ev, U = np.linalg.eigh((M + M.T) / 2)
    o = np.argsort(-ev)
    return ev[o], (Z - Z.mean(axis=0)) @ (Wh @ U[:, o])

LAG = 20                                              # frames = 40 ps
ev, Yt = tica(Y[:, :10], run_of, LAG)
its = -LAG * DT / np.log(np.clip(ev[:4], 1e-9, 0.999))
print("tICA at lag %d ps: eigenvalues %s" % (LAG * DT, np.round(ev[:4], 3)))

The left panel is the figure a student is most tempted to over-interpret. It does not show "the free-energy landscape of Trp-cage at two temperatures"; it shows that each 1 ns run visited one region and that the regions differ between runs of the same condition as much as between conditions. The tICA timescales say the same thing numerically: the slowest implied timescale at a 40 ps lag is about 177 ps, a fifth of the trajectory length, and estimates of implied timescales become unreliable once they approach the simulation length. A converged ensemble would show the six clouds overlapping, which is the practical convergence test to apply before any landscape is published[18][21].

9. A two-dimensional histogram is not a free-energy surface until it has error bars

Given an equilibrium ensemble, the probability $P(x,y)$ of being in a bin of a projection is related to a free energy by $F = -k_BT \ln P$ (up to an additive constant), with $k_BT = 2.49$ kJ/mol at 300 K. Two conditions must hold for that equation to mean anything: the sampling must be at equilibrium, and each bin must contain enough independent frames for $P$ to be estimated. Section 2 showed we have at most 28 independent frames per run, so the second condition is already in trouble. The remedy is to estimate the uncertainty of $F$ the same way the mean was estimated - by resampling whole blocks of frames with the bootstrap[33], which preserves the correlation inside a block.

kT = 0.0083145 * 300.0            # kJ/mol at 300 K
H, xe, ye = np.histogram2d(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], bins=30)
P = H / H.sum()
F = -kT * np.log(np.where(P > 0, P, np.nan)); F -= np.nanmin(F)

blocks = [np.where(run_of == r)[0][i:i + 50] for r in RUNS for i in range(0, 500, 50)]   # 100 ps blocks
rng_b = np.random.default_rng(0)
Fs = []
for _ in range(100):
    pick = np.concatenate([blocks[i] for i in rng_b.integers(0, len(blocks), len(blocks))])
    h, _, _ = np.histogram2d(Y[pick, 0], Y[pick, 1], bins=[xe, ye])
    p = h / h.sum()
    f = -kT * np.log(np.where(p > 0, p, np.nan))
    Fs.append(f - np.nanmin(f))
sdF = np.nanstd(np.array(Fs), axis=0)
well = np.isfinite(F) & (H >= 20)
print("occupied bins: %d of 900 | bins with >= 20 frames: %d" % (np.isfinite(F).sum(), well.sum()))
print("apparent depth using ALL occupied bins: %.1f kJ/mol (this is the number not to quote)" % np.nanmax(F))
print("free-energy range over well-populated bins: %.2f kJ/mol" % (np.nanmax(F[well]) - np.nanmin(F[well])))
print("bootstrap-over-blocks uncertainty there: median %.2f kJ/mol, maximum %.2f kJ/mol"
      % (np.nanmedian(sdF[well]), np.nanmax(sdF[well])))
print("ratio of the deepest apparent barrier to its own uncertainty: %.1f"
      % ((np.nanmax(F[well]) - np.nanmin(F[well])) / np.nanmedian(sdF[well])))

Figure 8. Left: the two-dimensional histogram of the pooled 3,000 frames converted to -kT ln P. It looks like a landscape with several minima separated by barriers of up to 10 kJ/mol. Right: the standard deviation of the same quantity over 100 bootstrap resamples of 100 ps blocks, restricted to bins with at least 20 frames. The uncertainty is about 1 kJ/mol over a usable range of 2.5 kJ/mol - the apparent structure is between two and three standard deviations deep, and the sparsely populated regions that carry the deepest "barriers" have no meaningful uncertainty at all because single blocks decide whether they are occupied.

Three rules follow, and they apply equally to the free-energy surfaces the group publishes for larger systems. Mask bins below a stated occupancy instead of letting one frame create a minimum. Attach an uncertainty obtained by resampling blocks (or, better, by comparing independent replicas) rather than frames. And never convert a histogram to a free energy when the ensemble is not equilibrium sampling - after a biased or steered simulation the transformation requires reweighting, which is the business of enhanced-sampling methods[28].

10. Clustering frames and extracting representative structures

Clustering a trajectory serves a practical purpose: to replace 3,000 frames by a handful of structures that can be drawn in a figure, docked, or submitted as supplementary coordinates. The algorithm is the k-means of Unit 15 applied to the projection, and the representative of a cluster is the frame closest to its centre. The diagnostic that matters is not the silhouette score but the cross-tabulation of clusters against runs.

km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Y[:, :5])
ct = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(run_of, name="run"), pd.Series(km.labels_, name="cluster"))
print(ct.to_string())
print()
for k in range(4):
    m = np.where(km.labels_ == k)[0]
    rep = m[np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(Y[m, :5] - km.cluster_centers_[k], axis=1))]
    print("cluster %d: %4d frames (%4.1f %%) | representative: run %s at %4d ps | RMSD there %.3f nm | runs present: %s"

Figure 9. Left: how the frames of each run distribute over the four clusters. Run A2 is entirely in cluster 0, A3 entirely in cluster 1, A1 almost entirely in cluster 2 and B1 94 % in the same cluster; only B2 (313/187) and B3 (330/162) are genuinely split between two clusters. A clustering that recovers the replica labels is reporting that the ensemble is not converged, not that the protein has four metastable states. Published as "the four dominant conformational states of Trp-cage", it would be an artefact; published as "each 1 ns replica remains within one basin, and the basins differ between replicas", it is a correct and useful statement about sampling. The representative structures are still perfectly usable as illustrations - cluster 2, sampled by both A1 and B1, is the most native-like with RMSD 0.106 nm - provided the caption says they are representatives of what was sampled rather than of equilibrium populations. A cluster population is only an equilibrium probability if the ensemble is converged, which here it is not.

11. Reporting an energy decomposition

Binding-free-energy estimates of the MM/PBSA and MM/GBSA family[9] are computed frame by frame and are usually accompanied by a per-residue decomposition. Everything in this unit applies to them, and more sharply, because the numbers are large and their differences are small. Three requirements are not optional. First, the error bar on a mean interaction energy must come from independent blocks or replicas, never from $\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{frames}}}$: energies decorrelate fast but the conformations that generate them do not. Second, a per-residue table of 200 residues compared between two systems is 200 simultaneous tests and needs the false-discovery-rate control of section 7; the usual presentation, a bar chart of the ten largest contributions, is a selection effect by construction. Third, the absolute value of an MM/GBSA energy is not a binding free energy - comparisons within one system and one protocol are defensible, comparisons across protocols are not. A reviewer who sees "ligand A: -45.2 +/- 0.3 kcal/mol, ligand B: -43.8 +/- 0.3 kcal/mol, therefore A binds better" is reading a standard error computed over correlated frames of a single trajectory, and the correct response is to ask for the replicas.

12. Summary

Six real nanosecond trajectories of a 20-residue protein were analysed here with no simulation software, only the frozen tables they produced. The accounting came first: the integrated autocorrelation time of the C-alpha RMSD is 18 to 85 ps depending on the replica, so each run of 500 stored frames contains between 5.9 and 27.6 independent configurations and the naive standard error is too small by a factor of 4.3 to 9.2. Block averaging agreed with the autocorrelation estimate where both could be computed, and the Flyvbjerg-Petersen curves never reached a plateau - the data telling us that 1 ns does not resolve the slowest contributing motion. Equilibration detection by reverse cumulative averaging and by Chodera's effective-sample-size criterion moved the means by at most 0.013 nm, so all frames were kept, and that decision was taken before any comparison.

Then the central experiment. Pooling frames, the two temperatures differ in C-alpha RMSD with p of order 1e-26; comparing the three replica means per condition, the same data give p = 0.69, with condition means of 0.174 +/- 0.041 and 0.153 +/- 0.019 nm. The 300 K replicas alone span 0.110 to 0.251 nm, a spread seven times the difference between the conditions. Four more structural observables behave identically - frame-level p-values between 1e-12 and 1e-30, replica-level p-values between 0.36 and 0.88 - while the thermostat and barostat readouts are significant by both routes (300.43 +/- 0.22 K against 340.24 +/- 0.07 K; 47.76 against 48.84 nm3), proving that n = 3 is not the obstacle. A power calculation on the replica spread says that detecting a 0.05 nm difference would need about sixteen replicas, and a 0.02 nm difference about a hundred.

The same discipline reshaped every downstream analysis. Per-residue RMSF rose by 25 % on average at 340 K (0.059 to 0.074 nm) yet no residue of twenty reached raw p < 0.05, let alone an FDR-corrected one. PCA put the six runs in six nearly disjoint islands and tICA at a 40 ps lag separated them further, with a slowest implied timescale of 177 ps - a fifth of the run length. The -kT ln P surface built from the pooled frames showed apparent minima of 10 kJ/mol, but a bootstrap over 100 ps blocks gave an uncertainty near 1 kJ/mol over a defensible range of only 2.5 kJ/mol. k-means on the projection returned four clean clusters that are, almost exactly, the six replicas. None of this means the simulations were useless: it means that what 1 ns x 6 supports is a description of what was sampled, error bars built from replicas, and an honest statement of what could not be resolved. The three habits to carry away are to quote $N_{\text{eff}}$ whenever an MD average is reported, to make the replica the unit of analysis in every test, and to put the uncertainty of a landscape or an energy decomposition next to the landscape itself[1][2][27]. Microsecond studies of this same protein[19][20] exist precisely because the honest analysis of a nanosecond says so little.

Within this course: the confidence intervals and the bootstrap come from Unit 7, the tests, power and FDR control from Unit 8, PCA from Unit 13, k-means from Unit 15, and the figure standards for the plots produced here from Unit 23; the compute side of running many replicas is Unit 25. The previous unit, Unit 19, treated the output of a screening pipeline with the same attitude. In the sister courses: how these trajectories are produced, from structure preparation to thermostats, is BGM324 unit 5 (Molecular dynamics), with the structural background in BGM324 unit 2; the free-energy and docking context is in BGM324 unit 4.

13. Self-assessment

1. A paper reports "RMSD = 0.21 +/- 0.01 nm (mean +/- SEM over 5,000 frames)". What is wrong, and what would you ask for?

The standard error was computed as sigma/sqrt(N_frames), which assumes independent frames. With an autocorrelation time of tens of picoseconds the effective sample size is one or two orders of magnitude smaller, so the quoted uncertainty is too small by sqrt(g). Ask for the integrated autocorrelation time or N_eff, a block-averaging plot, or - best - the per-replica means and an error bar built from them.

2. Why does saving frames more often make a frame-level t-test "more significant" without adding information?

Because the test's n is the number of saved frames, while the information content is set by the number of independent configurations, N_eff = N/g. Halving the output interval doubles N and leaves N_eff unchanged, so the p-value falls while nothing has been learnt. This is pseudo-replication.

3. State the difference between the statistical inefficiency g and the integrated autocorrelation time, and why two papers can report autocorrelation times differing by a factor of two.

g = 1 + 2 sum_k C(k) is dimensionless and equals the number of frames per independent sample; tau_int = dt(1/2 + sum_k C(k)) has units of time and satisfies g = 2 tau_int/dt. Some software reports dt(1 + 2 sum C(k)) = g dt instead, which is exactly twice tau_int - the factor of two seen between our table and the frozen summary file. Always give the definition or report N_eff.

4. Your Flyvbjerg-Petersen curve rises monotonically and never plateaus. What are your options?

The run is shorter than the slowest motion affecting the observable. Extend it, add independent replicas and build the error bar from the replica means, or restrict the claim to an observable that does decorrelate within the run. Reporting the last computable block value as "the" error bar understates the uncertainty.

5. Four of six runs need no equilibration discard and two need 300-550 ps. Should you discard the same amount from every run?

Applying a common, pre-registered discard (for instance the first 100 ps of every run) is defensible and simple; applying a per-run automated criterion is also defensible. What is not defensible is choosing per-run discards after seeing how they affect the comparison between conditions. Decide the rule first, report it, and show that the conclusion does not depend on it.

6. With three replicas per condition the temperature difference is detected at p of order 1e-6 but the RMSD difference is not detected at all. What does that prove?

That n = 3 is not inherently powerless: when the effect is large relative to the between-replica spread, three replicas suffice. The failure to detect an RMSD difference is therefore evidence that the structural effect is small compared with replica-to-replica variation at 1 ns, not evidence that the test is too weak to be used.

7. How many replicas would you request to detect a 0.05 nm difference in mean RMSD, and what did that estimate assume?

About sixteen per condition, from the observed between-replica standard deviation of 0.050 nm, 80 % power and a two-sided 5 % level. It assumes that the replica means are approximately normal and that the spread observed with three replicas is a reasonable estimate - itself uncertain with so few degrees of freedom, so treat the number as an order of magnitude.

8. A PCA plot shows two separated clouds for two trajectories of the same system. Name two innocent explanations before "two conformational states".

Insufficient sampling - each run relaxed into a different basin and never crossed back, which is exactly what Figure 7 shows - and the projection itself, since the leading components are chosen to maximise the variance that happens to be present, so any slow drift becomes PC1. A convergence check is whether independent replicas overlap in the projection.

9. What must accompany a -kT ln P landscape for it to be interpretable?

The occupancy threshold used to mask sparse bins, an uncertainty estimated by resampling blocks or by comparing replicas, a statement that the sampling is unbiased equilibrium sampling (or the reweighting scheme if it is not), and the temperature used in kT. Here the uncertainty was about 1 kJ/mol against a usable depth of 2.5 kJ/mol.

10. k-means on your trajectory projection returns clusters that coincide with the replicas. What do you report?

That the ensemble is not converged: each replica remained in its own basin. The representative structures may still be shown as illustrations of what was sampled, but cluster populations must not be presented as equilibrium probabilities, and the number of clusters must not be presented as a number of metastable states.

11. A collaborator sends a per-residue MM/GBSA decomposition for two ligands and asks which residues differ. What do you do first?

Count the tests. A 200-residue table is 200 comparisons; control the false-discovery rate, use replica-level or block-level error bars rather than per-frame ones, and refuse to interpret the ten largest bars as a finding, since selecting them after looking is a selection effect. Report effect sizes with intervals, not stars.

12. Summarise in one sentence what determines how strong a claim a set of simulations can support.

The number of independent samples - replicas first, then effectively independent configurations within each replica - and not the number of frames written to disk.

Glossary

Frame
One set of coordinates saved from a trajectory; here one every 2 ps, 500 per run.
Replica
An independent repetition of a simulation with a different random seed; the experimental unit for statistics.
RMSD
Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions from a reference after optimal superposition; a measure of how far a structure has moved.
RMSF
Root-mean-square fluctuation of a residue around its own mean position; a measure of local flexibility.
Autocorrelation function C(k)
Normalised correlation between a series and itself k steps later; C(0) = 1.
Integrated autocorrelation time
tau_int = dt(1/2 + sum_k C(k)); the time scale over which the series loses memory.
Statistical inefficiency g
1 + 2 sum_k C(k) = 2 tau_int/dt; the number of frames needed per independent sample.
Effective sample size
N_eff = N/g; the number of independent observations a correlated series is worth.
Block averaging
Estimating the standard error from the means of consecutive blocks; the estimate plateaus once blocks exceed the correlation time.
Flyvbjerg-Petersen plot
Block-averaged standard error against block length; absence of a plateau means the run is too short.
Equilibration detection
Choosing the portion of a run to discard, e.g. by reverse cumulative averaging or by maximising the retained effective sample size.
Pseudo-replication
Treating correlated observations (frames) as independent experimental units, inflating n and deflating p-values.
Essential dynamics / PCA
Principal component analysis of atomic coordinates; the leading components are the directions of largest positional variance.
tICA
Time-lagged independent component analysis: the linear projection maximising autocorrelation at a chosen lag, hence the slowest collective coordinates.
Implied timescale
-lag/ln(eigenvalue); an estimate of a relaxation time, trustworthy only when much shorter than the trajectory.
Free-energy surface
-kT ln P over a projection; meaningful only for equilibrium sampling, with masked sparse bins and a stated uncertainty.
MM/GBSA
End-point method estimating interaction energies frame by frame from a molecular-mechanics energy plus an implicit-solvent term; relative use within one protocol only.

Textbooks

  • Leach AR. Molecular Modelling: Principles and Applications. 2nd ed. Pearson; 2001. - Chapters 6-7 for the mechanics behind the trajectories analysed here.
  • Tuckerman ME. Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Molecular Simulation. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press; 2023. - Ensembles, thermostats and the meaning of a free-energy surface.
  • Wasserman L. All of Statistics. Springer; 2004. - Chapter 8 for the bootstrap used on blocks here.
  • VanderPlas J. Python Data Science Handbook. 2nd ed. O'Reilly; 2022. - NumPy and matplotlib idioms used throughout.

Online resources

  • MDAnalysis user guide and tutorials: userguide.mdanalysis.org.
  • MDTraj documentation: mdtraj.org.
  • pymbar, the reference implementation of equilibration detection and statistical inefficiency: pymbar.readthedocs.io.
  • LiveCoMS best-practices collection for molecular simulation: livecomsjournal.org.
  • OpenMM user guide, the engine that produced these trajectories: docs.openmm.org.
